_comment: Reference material for plant care and condition management. This is static agronomic text shown ALONGSIDE an analysis - it never influences what the analysis finds. Chemical entries name widely-documented active-ingredient CLASSES only: no product names, no dosages, no application rates. Every chemical entry requires the user to verify crop-specific registration against the product label and local regulations.
chemical_disclaimer: This names categories of active ingredient that are commonly documented for this type of problem. It is NOT a product recommendation and contains no dosages. Before using any product you must confirm it is registered for your specific crop in your country, read the label, observe the pre-harvest interval, and follow local regulations. If you are unsure of the diagnosis, do not apply a chemical treatment - use the cultural and organic measures instead.

immediate_actions: Do not apply any chemical treatment yet - an unconfirmed diagnosis is the most common reason a treatment fails
Remove and bin (do not compost) the worst-affected leaves to reduce spread and make monitoring easier
Isolate the plant from healthy neighbours if it is in a pot
Photograph the same leaf again in three to five days to see whether symptoms progress, stay static, or fade
organic_options: Improve airflow by thinning crowded growth and increasing spacing
Water at the soil surface rather than over the foliage, and water early in the day so leaves dry
Clear fallen leaves and debris from around the base of the plant
Keep tools and hands clean between plants
cultural_controls: Check soil moisture at root depth - both drought and waterlogging produce leaf symptoms
Review recent changes: new fertiliser, repotting, a move into stronger sun, a cold night
Inspect leaf undersides and new growth, where most problems appear first
prevention: Scout weekly and act on the first symptoms rather than waiting
Avoid overhead watering late in the day
Rotate annual crops and remove debris at the end of the season

immediate_actions: No treatment is needed for this leaf
cultural_controls: Continue the current watering and feeding routine
Keep scouting weekly, especially leaf undersides and lower foliage
prevention: Maintain airflow between plants
Water at the base, early in the day
Remove fallen debris to limit overwintering spores

immediate_actions: Pick off and bin the spotted leaves - do not compost them
Stop overhead watering; spots spread by water splash
Space or thin the plant so foliage dries quickly after rain or dew
organic_options: Mulch the soil surface to stop rain splashing spores up onto leaves
Neem oil or a potassium bicarbonate spray, applied to dry foliage out of direct sun
Biological fungicides based on Bacillus subtilis as a protectant on new growth
cultural_controls: Switch to drip or base watering
Prune the lowest leaves to raise the canopy away from the soil
Rotate annual crops away from the same family for two to three seasons
Clear and destroy all crop residue at the end of the season
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Avoid working among plants while the foliage is wet
Choose resistant varieties where available

immediate_actions: Remove affected leaves and bin them; disinfect tools afterwards
Stop all overhead watering immediately
Do not handle or harvest the plant while the foliage is wet - this is how it spreads fastest
organic_options: Copper-based products are the main organically-acceptable option, used preventively on unaffected growth
Improve air movement to shorten leaf wetness periods
cultural_controls: Use certified pathogen-free seed; hot-water seed treatment is standard for some crops
Rotate out of the affected family for at least a year
Remove volunteer and weed hosts nearby
Increase spacing to reduce humidity in the canopy

active_ingredient_classes: copper-based bactericides, often tank-mixed with mancozeb

prevention: Start with clean seed and transplants - this disease is usually introduced, not local
Avoid splashing water between plants
Sanitise trays, tools and stakes between seasons

immediate_actions: Remove and bin the affected lower leaves
Mulch the soil to block spore splash from debris
Check that the plant is not nitrogen-starved, which accelerates lower-leaf loss
organic_options: Copper-based protectant sprays on healthy foliage
Bacillus subtilis biofungicides as a preventive on new growth
Thick organic mulch to break the soil-to-leaf spore cycle
cultural_controls: Stake or cage plants to lift foliage off the ground
Water at the base, early in the day
Maintain balanced nutrition to delay leaf senescence
Rotate away from tomato, potato and other solanaceous crops for two to three seasons
prevention: Destroy cull piles and volunteer plants
Choose resistant or tolerant varieties
Remove crop debris completely after harvest

immediate_actions: Treat as urgent: this can destroy a planting within days in cool, wet weather
Remove and destroy infected plants away from the growing area - bag them, do not compost
Stop overhead irrigation entirely
Inspect every plant in the planting today, not just this one
organic_options: Copper-based products, applied preventively to unaffected plants - organic options are only protective, not curative
Remove lower leaves and increase spacing to reduce humidity
In severe outbreaks, destroying the crop early is often the only effective organic response
cultural_controls: Plant certified seed and resistant varieties - this is the main durable control
Avoid dense canopies that stay wet
Destroy the haulm before harvest to protect tubers in potato
Never leave cull piles near the growing area
prevention: Monitor local late blight forecasts during cool, wet periods
Use resistant cultivars where available
Source seed potatoes and transplants from certified suppliers only

immediate_actions: Improve airflow: thin crowded shoots and increase spacing
Remove the worst-affected leaves
Move potted plants out of deep shade into brighter, better-ventilated positions
organic_options: Potassium bicarbonate sprays, which also have some curative effect
Sulphur-based products - but not in hot weather and never close to an oil application
Neem oil or horticultural oil on dry foliage, out of direct sun
Milk-based sprays are a widely used home remedy with modest, variable results
cultural_controls: Reduce humidity around the foliage; avoid crowding
Avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which produces susceptible soft growth
Water at the base - unlike most fungi, powdery mildew does not need wet leaves
Prune for an open canopy
prevention: Choose resistant varieties - the difference is substantial for roses, grapes and cucurbits
Space plants for airflow at planting time
Remove and destroy infected debris at the end of the season

immediate_actions: Remove affected leaves and bin them
Stop overhead watering and avoid wetting foliage in the evening
Increase ventilation, especially in a greenhouse or polyhouse
organic_options: Copper-based protectant sprays on unaffected growth
Drastically reduce leaf wetness duration - this is more effective than any spray
Wider spacing and shoot thinning to cut canopy humidity
cultural_controls: Water early in the day so leaves dry before nightfall
Orient rows with the prevailing wind where possible
Remove and destroy infected debris
Rotate annual crops
prevention: Use resistant cultivars where they exist
Avoid dense, shaded plantings
Monitor during cool, humid weather, which is when it establishes

immediate_actions: Remove and bin affected leaves - do not shake them, which disperses spores
Avoid wetting the foliage
Clear fallen infected leaves from around the plant
organic_options: Sulphur-based products applied early, before pustules are widespread
Neem oil as a protectant on new growth
Thorough removal and destruction of infected leaves and debris
cultural_controls: Increase spacing and prune for airflow
Water at the base, early in the day
Remove nearby alternate host plants where the rust species requires one
Avoid excessive nitrogen
prevention: Plant resistant varieties - particularly effective for roses and beans
Clear all fallen leaves at the end of the season
Keep foliage dry

immediate_actions: Prune out affected leaves, shoots and fruit, and bin them
Disinfect pruning tools between cuts
Stop overhead watering
organic_options: Copper-based protectant sprays during wet weather
Remove all mummified fruit and infected twigs, which are the main overwintering source
Improve airflow through pruning
cultural_controls: Prune in dry weather only
Remove fallen fruit and leaf litter
Avoid wounding plants during wet conditions
Rotate annual crops and use clean seed
prevention: Sanitation is the main control: remove all infected plant material
Choose resistant varieties for mango, chilli and beans where available
Avoid dense canopies that hold moisture

immediate_actions: Check soil moisture at root depth, not at the surface - both drought and waterlogging cause this
Move potted plants out of harsh afternoon sun and drying wind
Stop fertilising until the cause is identified; salt build-up is a common cause
Flush pots thoroughly with clean water if over-fertilising is suspected
organic_options: Mulch to stabilise soil moisture and temperature
Water deeply and less often rather than little and often
Improve soil structure with compost so it holds moisture without waterlogging
cultural_controls: Check that pots drain freely and are not root-bound
Use collected rainwater if your tap water is hard or softened
Provide wind protection or afternoon shade for sensitive plants
Acclimatise plants gradually when moving them into stronger light
prevention: Water consistently - the irregular wet-dry cycle causes much of this damage
Fertilise at the recommended strength and no more
Match the plant to the position rather than fighting the position

immediate_actions: Isolate the plant from healthy ones immediately
Wash hands and disinfect tools after touching it - these viruses spread mechanically
Do not take cuttings or save seed from this plant
Confirm the plant is not simply a variegated cultivar before acting
organic_options: There is no cure for a virus-infected plant. Management means limiting spread
Control insect vectors - aphids, whiteflies and thrips - with insecticidal soap or neem oil
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce vector populations
Remove and destroy confirmed infected plants to protect the rest
cultural_controls: Use certified virus-free seed and planting material
Control weeds, which often harbour both virus and vectors
Avoid handling plants unnecessarily; never smoke or handle tobacco near solanaceous crops
Use insect-proof netting at the nursery stage
prevention: Plant resistant varieties where they exist - this is the only reliable protection
Manage the insect vectors rather than the virus
Sanitise tools, trays and stakes between plants and seasons

immediate_actions: Find the pest before treating: inspect undersides, leaf axils and new growth, and check at dusk
Hand-pick caterpillars, beetles, slugs and snails where numbers are small
Remove badly chewed leaves if they are no longer functional
organic_options: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil for soft-bodied insects, applied to the undersides
Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) for caterpillars specifically - it does not affect other insects
Neem oil as a feeding deterrent and growth regulator
Encourage predators: ladybirds, lacewings, parasitic wasps and birds
Physical barriers - netting, collars, copper tape for slugs
cultural_controls: Keep the area free of debris where pests shelter
Water in the morning so the surface is dry at night when slugs feed
Avoid excess nitrogen, which produces soft growth pests prefer
Rotate crops to break pest life cycles
prevention: Scout weekly - early small populations are far easier to manage
Use floating row covers on vulnerable young plants
Support natural predators by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides

immediate_actions: Identify the pattern before feeding: which leaves, and are the veins still green?
Check soil moisture - waterlogged roots cannot take up nutrients that are present
Do not apply a heavy dose of fertiliser as a guess; it can worsen the problem
organic_options: Well-rotted compost or worm castings for a broad, slow nutrient supply
Seaweed or fish-based liquid feeds for a gentle general correction
Composted manure worked into the surface for nitrogen over time
Adjust pH gradually with lime or elemental sulphur based on a soil test
cultural_controls: Test soil pH: most nutrients become unavailable outside pH 6.0-7.0 even when present
Improve drainage and soil structure so roots can function
Mulch to stabilise soil moisture and feed soil biology
Repot root-bound container plants into fresh medium

active_ingredient_classes: chelated iron (for interveinal yellowing on new growth)
magnesium sulphate (for interveinal yellowing on older leaves)

prevention: Feed according to the plant's growth stage rather than on a fixed schedule
Test soil every year or two rather than guessing
Maintain organic matter, which buffers nutrient availability

immediate_actions: Remove the old leaf if you prefer - this is normal ageing, not a problem to treat
cultural_controls: Confirm new growth is healthy; if it is, no action is needed
If many leaves are ageing at once, check watering and feeding
prevention: Keep nutrition steady through the growing season to delay leaf drop
Remove spent leaves to reduce places where pathogens overwinter

care.watering: Deep but infrequent. Allow the top of the soil to dry between waterings; mature trees are drought-tolerant and resent constantly wet roots. Reduce water during flowering to improve fruit set.
care.soil: Deep, free-draining loam, pH 5.5-7.5. Will not tolerate waterlogging - plant on a mound in heavy soil.
care.light: Full sun, at least six hours daily.
care.feeding: Feed after harvest and before flowering. Avoid heavy nitrogen close to flowering, which pushes leaf growth at the expense of fruit.
care.pruning: Open the canopy after harvest to improve airflow, which is the main cultural control for anthracnose and mildew.

prevention: Prune for an open canopy - anthracnose thrives in still, humid air
Collect and destroy fallen fruit and leaves
Avoid overhead irrigation during flowering

care.watering: Very drought-tolerant once established. Water young trees regularly for the first two seasons, then only in extended dry spells. Overwatering is the usual cause of problems.
care.soil: Tolerates poor, sandy and rocky soils. Needs good drainage; will not survive waterlogging.
care.feeding: Rarely needs feeding. A little compost annually is sufficient.
care.pruning: Prune to shape in the dry season; remove dead wood.

prevention: Avoid overwatering, which is the most common cause of decline
Keep the base clear of debris
Ensure free drainage

care.watering: Deep watering at the base, two or three times a week in dry weather. Never wet the foliage - black spot and mildew both depend on leaf wetness or humidity.
care.soil: Rich, well-drained loam, pH 6.0-6.5. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist.
care.light: At least six hours of direct sun; morning sun is ideal because it dries dew early.
care.feeding: Feed at the start of growth and after each flush of flowers. Stop feeding well before dormancy.
care.pruning: Prune hard in late dormancy to an open vase shape. Airflow through the centre is the single most effective disease control for roses.

prevention: Choose disease-resistant varieties - the difference in black spot and mildew is dramatic
Water at the base, early in the day
Clear fallen leaves, which carry black spot spores over winter
Space plants so air moves freely between them

care.watering: Keep evenly moist in the growing season - hibiscus wilts and drops buds quickly if it dries out. Reduce in cool weather.
care.soil: Rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, pH 6.0-6.8.
care.light: Full sun to light afternoon shade in very hot climates.
care.feeding: Needs regular potassium-rich feeding during flowering. Yellowing leaves on hibiscus are very often a feeding or watering issue rather than disease.
care.pruning: Pinch tips to encourage branching; prune in early spring.

prevention: Check leaf undersides regularly for aphids, whitefly and mealybug
Maintain even moisture - fluctuation causes leaf drop and yellowing
Feed consistently through the flowering season

care.watering: Heavy and consistent - bananas are very thirsty, but roots must not sit in standing water. Mulch heavily to retain moisture.
care.soil: Deep, rich, free-draining soil high in organic matter, pH 5.5-7.0.
care.light: Full sun, with shelter from strong wind which shreds the leaves.
care.feeding: Needs generous potassium and nitrogen through the growing season.
care.pruning: Remove dead and badly spotted leaves at the base to reduce disease pressure and improve airflow.

prevention: Remove old and infected leaves promptly - Sigatoka leaf spots build up on retained foliage
Provide wind shelter; torn leaves are entry points
Avoid overhead irrigation and maintain spacing

care.watering: Regular but very well drained - papaya roots rot readily. Keep water away from the stem base.
care.soil: Light, rich, free-draining soil, pH 6.0-6.5. Plant on a mound in heavy soil.
care.feeding: Feed little and often through the growing season; papaya grows and fruits fast.
care.pruning: Remove lower dead leaves. Do not top the plant.

prevention: Control aphids, which transmit papaya ringspot virus - vector control is the only effective virus management
Remove virus-infected plants promptly to protect the rest
Never let water pool around the stem base

care.watering: Moderate and regular while fruiting; tolerates short dry spells once established.
care.soil: Adaptable, but prefers well-drained loam, pH 5.0-7.0.
care.feeding: Feed two or three times during the growing season.
care.pruning: Prune annually after harvest to keep the canopy open - guava rust is strongly favoured by humid, enclosed canopies.

prevention: Keep the canopy open by annual pruning
Collect and destroy fallen fruit, which harbours fruit fly and anthracnose
Avoid overhead watering in humid weather

care.watering: Deep weekly watering in dry weather, particularly while fruit is sizing. Avoid wetting foliage.
care.feeding: Feed in early spring before bud break. Avoid late-season nitrogen, which delays hardening.
care.pruning: Prune in dormancy to an open centre. Scab and mildew control depend heavily on airflow and light into the canopy.

prevention: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves, which carry apple scab through the winter
Choose scab-resistant cultivars where available
Prune annually for light and air

care.watering: Deep and infrequent. Grapes are deep-rooted and over-watering produces soft, disease-prone growth and poor fruit.
care.soil: Well-drained, moderately fertile soil, pH 6.0-6.8. Excellent drainage is essential.
care.light: Full sun, with good air movement through the canopy.
care.feeding: Modest feeding only; excess nitrogen strongly increases mildew susceptibility.
care.pruning: Prune hard in dormancy and thin leaves around fruit clusters during the season. Canopy management is the primary mildew control in grapes.

prevention: Thin the canopy to expose clusters to air and light
Train vines on a trellis for airflow
Remove and destroy prunings and mummified fruit
Monitor from bud break - both mildews establish early

care.watering: Deep and consistent at the base. Irregular watering causes blossom-end rot and splitting; wet foliage drives nearly every tomato leaf disease.
care.soil: Rich, free-draining soil, pH 6.0-6.8, with steady calcium availability.
care.light: Full sun, six to eight hours.
care.feeding: Balanced feeding early, then higher potassium once fruit sets. Excess nitrogen gives leaf growth and little fruit.
care.pruning: Remove the lowest leaves as the plant grows and stake or cage it. Lifting foliage off the soil is the single most effective blight measure.

prevention: Mulch to stop soil splash onto leaves
Stake and prune to lift and open the canopy
Rotate out of the solanaceous family for two to three seasons
Water at the base, early in the day
Remove all debris at the end of the season

care.watering: Consistent moisture while tubers form; avoid wetting foliage. Reduce water as the crop matures.
care.soil: Loose, free-draining soil, pH 5.0-6.5. Hill the soil up around stems as they grow.
care.feeding: Moderate nitrogen early; too much extends leafy growth and delays tubers.
care.pruning: Not pruned, but remove badly blighted foliage and destroy it away from the field.

prevention: Plant certified seed tubers - this is the main route late blight enters a crop
Hill adequately to protect developing tubers from spores washing down
Destroy cull piles and volunteer plants
Monitor blight forecasts in cool, wet weather

care.watering: Even moisture at the base; peppers drop flowers if they dry out or are waterlogged.
care.feeding: Balanced feeding; excess nitrogen gives leaves instead of fruit.
care.pruning: Light pruning only. Remove lower leaves touching the soil.

prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seed - bacterial spot is seed-borne
Never work among plants while the foliage is wet
Rotate crops and remove debris
Maintain spacing for airflow

care.watering: Consistent moisture, critical at tasselling and silking. Water at the base.
care.feeding: A heavy nitrogen feeder; side-dress during rapid growth. Pale lower leaves usually mean nitrogen, not disease.
care.pruning: Not pruned. Remove badly diseased lower leaves if infection is heavy.

prevention: Plant in blocks for pollination but maintain row spacing for airflow
Rotate out of corn to break rust and leaf blight cycles
Choose resistant hybrids where rust is a recurring problem
Incorporate or remove residue after harvest

care.watering: Deep watering when the top few centimetres dry. Citrus hates both drought and waterlogging; erratic watering causes leaf drop.
care.soil: Free-draining, slightly acidic soil, pH 6.0-7.0. Never let pots stand in water.
care.light: Full sun, at least six hours.
care.feeding: Citrus-specific feed with micronutrients during growth flushes. Interveinal yellowing on citrus is very often iron, zinc or manganese shortage rather than disease.
care.pruning: Remove dead wood, suckers below the graft, and crossing branches to open the canopy.

prevention: Feed with a citrus fertiliser containing micronutrients - deficiency is the most common cause of citrus leaf symptoms
Inspect new flushes for leaf miner and psyllid damage
Ensure free drainage
Avoid overhead watering

care.watering: Deep and regular, allowing the surface to dry between waterings. Avoid waterlogging.
care.feeding: Citrus feed with micronutrients, split across the growing season.
care.pruning: Light pruning to remove dead wood and open the canopy; avoid heavy cuts.

prevention: Feed with micronutrients to prevent the chlorosis that mimics disease
Monitor for citrus psyllid, which transmits serious citrus disease
Maintain drainage and avoid wetting foliage
Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves and fruit

care.watering: Water when the top two to three centimetres of soil feel dry, and water at the base rather than over the leaves. Most leaf problems are made worse by wet foliage, and most root problems by soil that never dries.
care.soil: Use a free-draining medium with organic matter. Check that pots drain freely and are not root-bound.
care.light: Match light to the plant: most flowering and fruiting plants want six or more hours of sun, most foliage plants prefer bright indirect light. Acclimatise gradually when moving a plant into stronger light.
care.feeding: Feed at the recommended strength during active growth only. Over-feeding causes salt burn, which looks like disease.
care.pruning: Remove dead and badly affected leaves, and thin crowded growth to improve airflow.

prevention: Identify the plant so that care and treatment can be matched to it
Water at the base, early in the day
Keep air moving around the foliage
Remove fallen leaves and debris
Inspect new growth and leaf undersides weekly
